title: Exercised control, lighting choices, and energy use: an office simulation experiment
research_question: Does individual control over workplace lighting lead to beneficial outcomes such as improved work performance, satisfaction, and reduced energy use, particularly when compared to working under identical lighting conditions without choice?

participants.description: 47 office workers in each condition (52 women, 42 men), ages 18-62, from a large Canadian city. Normal or corrected-to-normal vision, normal hearing, no mobility impairments, experience with Windows™-based word-processing and spreadsheets, and sufficient English fluency.
participants.recruitment: Recruited in 60 matched pairs (by age and sex) through two temporary-employment agencies.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Mocked-up 12.2 x 6.7 m (40 x 22 ft) windowless open-plan office with modular systems furniture (1.67 m partitions) providing six workstations. Only two center workstations were used. Hybrid lighting system with four controllable circuits: (1) recessed 1'x4' deep-cell parabolic louvered luminaires overhead (dimmable 10-100%), (2) recessed 1'x4' deep-cell parabolic louvered luminaires at perimeter (dimmable 10-100%), (3) partition-mounted indirect lighting (dimmable 30-100%), and (4) undershelf task lighting (on-off control). All lamps T8, 3500K CCT, CRI=80. Ambient noise at 48 dB(A).
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Setting and Lighting Conditions, Figure 1, Figure 2, Table 1

measures.instrument: Recorded dimmer settings for partition-mounted, perimeter parabolic, centre parabolic, and task lamp
Photometric measurements (LMM, average luminance, VDT screen glare luminance, desktop illuminance, maximum ceiling luminance)
VALID (Vision and Lighting Diagnostic test) scores
Custom software, time spent checking screen
Custom software, number of errors per screen

measures.construct: Physical symptoms (visual fatigue, physical symptoms, mental fatigue, nasal/throat symptoms)

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group)
findings.mechanism: Direct manipulation of lighting controls leads to a stronger belief in personal control over lighting.
findings.quote: CS participants perceived that they had had strong control over the lighting, whereas PP participants perceived themselves to have had no control over the lighting.

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group)
findings.mechanism: Having the opportunity to make lighting choices in the morning contributed to feeling more in control of events all day.
findings.quote: the difference between CS and PP participants on the Perceived Session Control is also a large effect in terms of variance explained.

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group vs PP group)
findings.quote: The multivariate test was significant, and examination of the univariate tests revealed that the effect was associated with differences on both the Perceived Session Control and the Lighting Control scale (Table 4).

findings.antecedent: Choice condition (CS group)
findings.consequent: Preference for making continuous adjustments over the course of a workday
findings.mechanism: CS participants knew that lighting changes had been made earlier in the day and no further changes had been permitted, leading to a higher reported preference for continuous adjustments.
findings.quote: CS participants reported a higher preference for making continuous adjustments over the course of a workday (M=3.19; SD=0.68) than PP participants (M=2.70; SD=0.79)

findings.antecedent: No choice condition (PP group)
findings.consequent: Importance of lighting in the workplace
findings.mechanism: PP participants, lacking control, may have perceived lighting as more important, possibly due to a desire for control.
findings.quote: PP participants reported giving greater importance to lighting in the workplace [F(1,89)= 6.21, p<.05; CS M=2.83 (SD=1.12), PP M=3.32 (SD=0.78)]

findings.antecedent: Experience with the space (PP group's end-of-day choice vs CS group's morning choice)
findings.mechanism: PP participants, after a day's experience, learned that lower output from perimeter parabolic luminaires reduced VDT glare.
findings.quote: PP participants, after a day's experience working the space, chose a lower output for this system than the CS participants when they made their choices in the morning.

findings.antecedent: Experience with the space (PP group's end-of-day choice vs CS group's morning choice)
findings.mechanism: PP participants' lower use of perimeter parabolic luminaires reduced the intensity of reflected luminaire images on the VDT screen.
findings.quote: The lower use of the perimeter parabolic luminaires by PP participants reduced the intensity of the reflected luminaire images in the VDT screen

findings.antecedent: Experience with the space (PP group's end-of-day choice vs CS group's morning choice)
findings.mechanism: PP participants' lower use of perimeter parabolic luminaires reduced overall power consumption.
findings.quote: and reduced overall power consumption.

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group vs PP group)
findings.mechanism: CS participants experienced greater visual fatigue, possibly due to the cognitive load of making choices or the specific choices made.
findings.quote: Afternoon VALID scores for the PP group (Madj= 60.02) were higher than those for the CS group (Madj= 58.20), indicating greater visual fatigue for CS than PP participants.

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group vs PP group)
findings.consequent: Creative writing task performance (speed, characters typed, word length, sentence length, grade level)
findings.mechanism: The non-stressful nature of the working conditions may have rendered the presence or absence of control unimportant for performance.
findings.quote: There were no significant multivariate effects; therefore, no univariate tests were interpreted (for Choice, Wilks' A=0.897, F(5,88)=2.02, n.s.)

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group vs PP group)
findings.consequent: Typing and proofreading task performance (speed, accuracy)
findings.mechanism: The non-stressful nature of the working conditions may have rendered the presence or absence of control unimportant for performance.
findings.quote: There were no effects for Choice (Wilks' A=0.901, F(5,88)=1.93, n.s)

findings.antecedent: Time of day (morning vs afternoon)
findings.mechanism: Learning effect over the course of the day.
findings.quote: Only the Session effect was statistically significant (Wilks' A=0.436, F(5,88)=22.75, p<.001). ... performance improved from the morning to the afternoon, which suggests a learning effect

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group vs PP group)
findings.consequent: Number of trials completed and duration of rest breaks
findings.quote: there were no Choice (Wilks' A=0.956, F(6,87)=0.68, n.s) or Choice X Session (Wilks' A=0.989, F(6,87)=0.16, n.s) effects

findings.antecedent: Time of day (morning vs afternoon)
findings.mechanism: Learning effect over the course of the day.
findings.quote: only the Session effect was statistically significant (Wilks' A=0.480, F(6,87)=15.71, p<.001). Participants completed more trials of all types in the afternoon than in the morning, which is consistent with the learning effect

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group vs PP group)
findings.quote: There were no significant differences; the two groups did not perceive the tasks differently, nor did they hold different views as to the effects of the physical environment on their productivity that day (Wilks' A=.934; F(7,85)=0.85, n.s.).

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group vs PP group)
findings.mechanism: The non-stressful nature of the working conditions may have rendered the presence or absence of control unimportant for mood.
findings.quote: Again, there were no Choice (Wilks' A=0.978, F(3,90)=0.69, n.s) or Session X Choice (Wilks' A=0.966, F(3,90)=1.06, n.s) effects.

findings.antecedent: Time of day (morning vs afternoon)
findings.mechanism: Participants felt less aroused, less pleasant, and less in control of the situation by the end of the afternoon session, indicating cognitive fatigue or general decline over the workday.
findings.quote: The only significant multivariate effect was the Session effect comparing morning and afternoon scores (Wilks' A=0.555, F(3,90)=24.10, p<.001), associated with significant univariate tests for all three scales. Scores on all three mood scales dropped from morning to afternoon

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group vs PP group)
findings.consequent: Environmental Satisfaction, Lighting Quality, and Glare
findings.mechanism: The non-stressful nature of the working conditions (low glare, high lighting quality, mild environmental satisfaction) may have rendered the presence or absence of control unimportant for satisfaction.
findings.quote: The multivariate test was not statistically significant (Wilks' A=.976, F(3,90)=0.73). There were no differences between CS and PP participants in terms of their satisfaction with the workplace nor with the lighting, including glare.

findings.antecedent: Availability of choice over lighting (CS group vs PP group)
findings.consequent: Incidence of physical symptoms (visual fatigue, physical symptoms, mental fatigue, nasal/throat symptoms)
findings.mechanism: The non-stressful nature of the working conditions may have rendered the presence or absence of control unimportant for physical symptoms.
findings.quote: The multivariate test was not statistically significant (Wilks' A =.975, F(4,89)=0.58). CS and PP participants did not differ in the incidence of physical symptoms over the course of the day.

findings.antecedent: Luminous conditions chosen by CS participants
findings.mechanism: 70% of CS participants chose desktop illuminance levels equal to or lower than the IESNA RP-1 (1993) level of 500 lx, indicating a preference for moderate light levels consistent with standards.
findings.quote: Seventy per cent of CS participants in this experiment chose desktop illuminance levels (measured away from the task lamp, and unobstructed in any way) equal to or lower than the IESNA RP-1 (1993) level of 500 lx (Figure 3).

findings.antecedent: Luminous conditions chosen by CS participants
findings.mechanism: The 75th percentile of energy consumption was within the limits of existing standards, suggesting that individual control does not necessarily lead to excessive energy use.
findings.quote: For CS participants, the 75th percentile of energy consumption was within the limits of existing standards in Canada and the United States (ASHRAE/IESNA, 1989; CCBFC, 1997), suggesting that these limits are not too low to satisfy most people.

mechanisms: The non-stressful nature of the working conditions: When environmental conditions are acceptably good, the presence or absence of control is unimportant for satisfaction, mood, performance, or health. Control is more beneficial in aversive or stressful conditions.
Learning and experience: Over time, individuals can learn what works and what needs correction in an environment, leading to more optimal choices (e.g., reducing glare) if control is available.

Cognitive load of choice: Making choices, especially under observation, might impose a cognitive load that could negatively impact performance or increase fatigue, as seen in the visual fatigue finding for CS participants.
moderators: Stressfulness of environmental conditions (implied by discussion of null results)
implementation_implications: Providing individual control over lighting does not necessarily lead to immediate benefits in satisfaction, mood, performance, or health in non-stressful, well-designed office environments.
Individual control over lighting does not necessarily lead to excessive energy use; participants tended to choose conditions consistent with or lower than current recommended practice.

Experience with the workspace can lead to more optimized lighting choices (e.g., reduced glare, lower energy consumption), suggesting that long-term control or learning opportunities could be beneficial.

Designers should consider providing individual control over lighting and other environmental features to foster feelings of environmental competence and perceived control, which may have longer-term benefits beyond immediate performance or satisfaction.

Careful lighting and interior design, appropriate training for using new systems, and quick response to problems are essential to avoid negative consequences of control, such as learned helplessness from failed attempts to optimize conditions.

limitations: The environmental conditions were generally good and non-stressful, which may have masked potential benefits of control that would be observed in less optimal conditions.
The experiment duration was one working day, which is shorter than typical employee exposure, potentially limiting the observation of long-term benefits of control or learning effects.
The informed-consent procedures, which allow participants to leave early, may obscure perceived control effects, as all participants technically have a choice.
The loss of participants reduced the theoretical power of the experiment to .67, making it possible that some medium-sized effects were not detected as statistically significant.
